title: How to Route Images Between Cheap and Expensive AI Models
summary: Route images between a cheap model and an expensive model with Roboflow Workflows: use detector confidence to send only hard cases to big VLMs.
body_markdown:
SUMMARY


**To route images between a cheap model and an expensive model, run a fast object detector like RF-DETR first, then use its classes and confidence scores to decide where each image goes. In Roboflow Workflows, you set those routing rules with conditional branches: high-confidence, routine results go to a lightweight model, while uncertain or high-priority cases go to a larger VLM or to a person. That way you pay for the expensive model only on the images that need it.**


Routing images between a cheap model and an expensive model helps control inference costs by choosing which model analyzes each image. Instead of sending every image to your most expensive[vision language model (VLM)](https://roboflow.com/blog/what-is-a-vision-language-model?ref=blog.roboflow.com) , you can use a lightweight detector’s predictions to route routine cases to a lower-cost model and reserve more expensive analysis for uncertain detections or priority defect classes. This approach is called model routing.


Consider a furniture[manufacturing](https://roboflow.com/industries/manufacturing?ref=blog.roboflow.com) line inspecting wooden panels before finishing. A familiar surface feature detected with high confidence may need only a lightweight check. A possible crack, missing knot, or low-confidence detection may warrant a different model. Routing rules make that choice explicit, using detected classes and confidence scores to select the next step.


In this guide, you’ll build an image-routing system in Roboflow Workflows using an RF-DETR Small detector and conditional logic. Each image will go to one of three Gemini models Flash-Lite, Flash, or Pro, or be flagged for human review. You’ll also validate model responses, flag disagreements, and collect selected images for retraining. Finally, you’ll learn what to measure to determine whether routing reduces total cost while meeting your inspection requirements.


## What Is Model Routing for Computer Vision?


Model routing for computer vision is the process of selecting which model should analyze an image using signals such as detected objects, confidence scores, or the task being performed. The goal is to choose a model that meets the application’s accuracy and latency requirements at the lowest practical cost.


For example, a lightweight object detector can inspect an image first and return the objects it found with their confidence scores. Routing rules then use those predictions to choose the next model. A routine detection might send the image to a cheaper vision language model (VLM), while a possible crack or an uncertain detection sends it to a more expensive model.


Model routing is related to image pre-filtering and sequential escalation. But each answers a different question:


Approach


Question it answers


Example


Image pre-filtering


Does this image need further analysis?


Send an image to a VLM only when a detector finds a wooden panel.


Model routing


Which model should analyze this image?


Select Flash-Lite, Flash, or Pro using detected classes and confidence scores.


Sequential escalation


Does the first model’s answer need another check?


Run a cheaper VLM, evaluate its response, and call another model if needed.


## How to Build an Image Model Router in Roboflow


We will build the inspection system,[wood-defect-model-router](https://app.roboflow.com/workflows/embed/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ3b3JrZmxvd0lkIjoibUc4M3Qwd21DM1NKSWpzWkFqYUYiLCJ3b3Jrc3BhY2VJZCI6InZjQmw1Y0x3bUtQallLTGNRemV1VkE4UlRhNjIiLCJ1c2VySWQiOiJ2Y0JsNWNMd21LUGpZS0xjUXpldVZBOFJUYTYyIiwiaWF0IjoxNzkyOTQ2NDc1fQ.ga9JZWKKt5xk4E2XXyIybfzqjIDRRW2BTqsSdzlP2Hs?ref=blog.roboflow.com) workflow, in Roboflow Workflows by connecting the detector, routing logic, model branches, and review checks. First, RF-DETR will locate surface features in the panel image. Property Definition blocks will extract the class names and confidence scores, and a[custom Python block (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/custom-blocks?ref=blog.roboflow.com) named` Routing_Signals` will validate the predictions. An Expression block will then choose a route, while Continue If gates will activate the selected branch.


For a Gemini route, the chosen model will analyze the original image. A JSON Parser will extract the response fields, and` Inspection_Branch` will group them with the model identifier and error flags. The human-review branch will use` Human_Result` to record that manual inspection is needed. First Non Empty Or Default will pass the result from the selected branch to` Inspection_Decision` , which will validate it, compare the detector and Gemini class sets when a Gemini response is available, and decide whether human review or image collection is needed.


Finally, visualization blocks will draw the detector boxes, class labels, and confidence scores, then add the selected route, model, and review flag. We will also add an optional Dataset Upload path to collect selected images for retraining and a Webhook Sink to send flagged cases to a review application. Figure 1 shows how these components connect.


**Figure 1. Wood-surface inspection workflow with conditional model routing.**


### Step 1: Define the Workflow inputs


Start with the image and the parameters that the Workflow needs for each inspection. Configure these four inputs:


Input Purpose Default


` image` Original image of the wooden panel Supplied for each inspection


` inspection_id` ID used to link the result to an inspection Supplied by the calling application


` detector_confidence` Minimum confidence for detections returned by the detector` 0.20`


` enable_collection` Allows selected images to enter the collection path` false`


Use an image input for` image` and parameter inputs for the other values. The calling application supplies` inspection_id` ; later blocks include it in the results and collection metadata. Keep` enable_collection=false` while checking the routing behavior, then enable it when you are ready to collect images.


### Step 2: Add the wood defect detector


Add an[Object Detection Model block (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/run-a-model/object-detection-model?ref=blog.roboflow.com) and name it` wood_detector` . We will use the trained RF-DETR Small model from project[wood-surface-defect-detection (opens in a new tab)](https://universe.roboflow.com/tim-4ijf0/wood-surface-defect-detection?ref=blog.roboflow.com) .


**Figure 2. project on Roboflow Universe.**


Configure the block with these settings:


Setting Value


Image` $inputs.image`


Model ID` tim-4ijf0/wood-surface-defect-detection-1-rfdetr-small-t1`


Confidence mode` custom`


Custom confidence` $inputs.detector_confidence`


The model supports eight surface classes:


` Crack` ,` Marrow` ,` Resin` ,` Dead_Knot` ,` Knot_with_Crack` ,` Quartzity` ,` Live_Knot` , and` Knot_Missing` .


Its output contains bounding boxes, class names, and individual confidence scores. Object detection is useful here because a single panel can contain several features or defects, each with its own location and score.


The initial cutoff of` 0.20` keeps lower-confidence detections available for routing. Predictions below this cutoff are still removed, so the router can inspect only the detections returned by the model.


### Step 3: Extract and validate the routing signals


Add two Property Definition blocks that read` $steps.wood_detector.predictions` . Name them` detector_classes` and` detector_confidences` . Use` DetectionsPropertyExtract` to extract` class_name` in the first block and` confidence` in the second.


Next, add a custom` Routing_Signals` block and name it` routing_signals` . Connect the original detector predictions to its` predictions` input, the extracted class names to` classes` , and the extracted confidence scores to` confidences` .


The block checks that the numbers of class names, confidence scores, and bounding boxes match the number of detections. It also checks that each class is supported, each score is a finite number between 0 and 1, and each box has finite coordinates with positive width and height. A finite value excludes NaN and infinity. Configure the block to return these six Boolean outputs:


Flag When it is true


` invalid` The prediction data fails validation or an exception occurs while checking it.


` critical` At least one` Crack` ,` Knot_with_Crack` , or` Knot_Missing` is present.


` low` At least one returned confidence is below` 0.60` .


` medium` At least one returned confidence is below` 0.90` .


` empty` A valid detector result contains zero detections.


` high` At least one detection exists and every returned confidence is at least` 0.90` .


The block starts with` invalid=true` and all other flags set to` false` . It sets the other flags only after the prediction data passes validation. Here,` critical` identifies the three classes given priority by our routing policy; it does not measure the panel’s physical strength or assign a wood grade.


Use the following code in the` routing_signals` Custom Python block:


Python


```text
def   run  (self, predictions, classes, confidences):
import   math
import   numpy   as   np


flags   =   {
"invalid"  :   True  ,
"critical"  :   False  ,
"low"  :   False  ,
"medium"  :   False  ,
"empty"  :   False  ,
"high"  :   False  ,
}


allowed   =   {
"Crack"  ,   "Marrow"  ,   "Resin"  ,   "Dead_Knot"  ,
"Knot_with_Crack"  ,   "Quartzity"  ,   "Live_Knot"  ,   "Knot_Missing"  ,
}
priority_classes   =   {  "Crack"  ,   "Knot_with_Crack"  ,   "Knot_Missing"  }


try  :
names   =   list  (classes)   if   classes   is   not   None   else   []
scores   =   list  (confidences)   if   confidences   is   not   None   else   []
boxes   =   predictions.xyxy
n   =   len  (predictions)


if   (
len  (names)   !=   n
or   len  (scores)   !=   n
or   boxes   is   None
or   len  (boxes)   !=   n
):
return   flags


for   name, score, box   in   zip  (names, scores, boxes):
if   (
not   isinstance  (name,   str  )
or   name   not   in   allowed
or   score   is   None
or   not   math.isfinite(  float  (score))
or   not   0   <=   float  (score)   <=   1
or   not   np.all(np.isfinite(box))
or   float  (box[  2  ])   <=   float  (box[  0  ])
or   float  (box[  3  ])   <=   float  (box[  1  ])
):
return   flags


flags.update(
invalid  =  False  ,
critical  =  any  (name   in   priority_classes   for   name   in   names),
low  =  any  (  float  (score)   <   0.60   for   score   in   scores),
medium  =  any  (  float  (score)   <   0.90   for   score   in   scores),
empty  =  n   ==   0  ,
high  =  n   >   0   and   all  (  float  (score)   >=   0.90   for   score   in   scores),
)


except   Exception  :
# Keep the invalid flag when prediction data cannot be checked.
pass


return   flags
```


These flags describe the detector’s results. In the next step, the` select_route` Expression block uses them to choose one route for the image.


### Step 4: Define which route each image takes


Add an[Expression block (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/advanced-blocks/expression?ref=blog.roboflow.com) named` select_route` . Connect the six flags from` routing_signals` and configure the cases in the following order. The first matching case determines the route for the entire image.


Order Condition Route value


1 Invalid prediction data or an unexpected class` human`


2 Any` Crack` ,` Knot_with_Crack` , or` Knot_Missing` , regardless of its returned confidence` pro`


3 Otherwise, any returned confidence below` 0.60`` pro`


4 Otherwise, any returned confidence below` 0.90`` flash`


5 Successful detector result with zero detections` flash_lite`


6 Otherwise, every returned confidence is at least` 0.90`` flash_lite`


Default No matching valid rule` human`


The order matters because some flags overlap. A confidence below` 0.60` also satisfies the` medium` flag, but the Pro rule is checked first. A priority class also selects Pro even when its confidence is high.


The router checks every detection separately and does not average confidence scores. One low-confidence detection can therefore change the route for the whole image, even when the other detections have high scores.


If the detector successfully returns no detections, Flash-Lite checks the complete image. An empty detection result alone does not establish that the panel is defect-free.


We will use` 0.60` and` 0.90` as initial routing thresholds in the custom code. The` 0.20` detector cutoff is a Workflow input. Adjust these values after evaluating the Workflow on your inspection images. If you change the routing thresholds, also update the matching routing-reason text in` Inspection_Decision` .


**Figure 3. Routing rules evaluated in priority order for each inspection image.**


We will use per-detection confidence scores as the numeric routing signal. The Gemini response contains classes, an assessment, and a reason; it does not contain a likelihood score. If you add a score from another model, check what it means and test whether it helps with routing before choosing thresholds. A confidence value requested in a VLM prompt should not automatically use the detector's thresholds.


A score returned by Gemini is available only after that model runs. It can support a later review decision, but it cannot decide whether to make the call that produced it.


### Step 5: Connect the Gemini and human-review branches


Add four[Continue If gates (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/logic-and-branching/continue-if?ref=blog.roboflow.com) . Each gate compares` $steps.select_route.output` with one route value. Set its` next_steps` connection to the first block in the matching branch:


Gate Route value Next step


` gate_flash_lite`` flash_lite`` inspect_flash_lite`


` gate_flash`` flash`` inspect_flash`


` gate_pro`` pro`` inspect_pro`


` gate_human`` human`` human_result`


For the first three branches, add a[Google Gemini block (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/run-a-model/google-gemini?ref=blog.roboflow.com) with the corresponding step name. Configure` model_version` for each branch as follows:


Branch Configured Gemini model


Flash-Lite` gemini-3.5-flash-lite`


Flash` gemini-3.8-flash`


Pro` gemini-3.1-pro-preview`


Check that all three models are available in the environment where you will run the Workflow.


Set each Gemini block's image input to` $inputs.image` and its task to` structured-answering` . For a Gemini route, the selected model receives the original image. The visualization blocks prepare the annotated output separately.


Configure all three Gemini blocks to request the same response fields:


Field Expected content


` visible_classes` A list containing supported class names, or an empty list.


` assessment` Exactly` visible_defect` ,` no_visible_defect` , or` unclear` .


` reason` A short explanation based on visible evidence.


Ask the model to identify the eight supported surface classes and return multiple classes when appropriate. It should return` unclear` when blur, glare, obstruction, or insufficient detail prevents a reliable assessment. Limit the model's answer to visible surface conditions and exclude judgments about internal strength or commercial wood grade.


For the human branch, use the custom` Human_Result` block named` human_result` . It creates a result with` model="none"` , an empty class list,` assessment="unclear"` , and the reason` Manual review required` . This records the need for a person to inspect the case; it does not perform that review.


### Step 6: Parse the response and join the branches


Connect each Gemini block to a[JSON Parser (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/advanced-blocks/json-parser?ref=blog.roboflow.com) , then to a custom` Inspection_Branch` block:


Gemini step JSON Parser Result block


` inspect_flash_lite`` parse_flash_lite`` result_flash_lite`


` inspect_flash`` parse_flash`` result_flash`


` inspect_pro`` parse_pro`` result_pro`


Each parser reads its Gemini block's output and extracts` visible_classes` ,` assessment` , and` reason` . It also exposes an error flag. Each` Inspection_Branch` block packages these fields, the model identifier, and the model/parser error flags into a` bundle` : a dictionary that keeps the related values together.


Next, add a[First Non Empty Or Default block (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/advanced-blocks/first-non-empty-or-default?ref=blog.roboflow.com) named` selected_result` . Connect the bundles from the three result blocks and` human_result` to its` data` input.


Only the selected branch supplies a result. The join passes that bundle to the next stage, giving the review logic a common structure to read. It does not combine answers from multiple Gemini models or run an ensemble.


Configure its default bundle with` model="none"` , an empty class list,` assessment="unclear"` , the reason` No branch completed` , and both error flags set to` true` . This marks a missing branch result as unavailable when execution reaches the join.


### Step 7: Validate the answer and decide whether review is needed


Add the custom` Inspection_Decision` block and name it` inspection_decision` . Connect the selected route, the bundle from` selected_result` , the detector predictions,` inspection_id` , and the` invalid` and` critical` routing flags.


The block first checks whether the route is recognized and whether` routing_signals` has marked the predictions as invalid. It skips reading predictions already marked as invalid. Otherwise, it reads the class names and confidence scores, checks that their counts match the number of detections, and verifies that the classes are supported and the scores are finite numbers between 0 and 1. If reading or validating this data fails, the case is flagged for review.


Next, the block checks Gemini’s response. The` visible_classes` field must be a list of supported class names,` assessment` must be` visible_defect` ,` no_visible_defect` , or` unclear` , and` reason` must be a nonempty string. The fields must also agree:` visible_defect` requires at least one class, while` no_visible_defect` requires an empty class list.


The block sets` needs_review=true` when any of these conditions applies:


- The route is` human` or unrecognized, or the detector predictions are invalid or cannot be read.
- The model or JSON Parser reports an error, or the response values fail validation.
- Gemini returns an` unclear` assessment.
- Gemini and the detector report different class sets.


For a valid Gemini response with no reported errors and valid detector data, the block compares distinct class sets. A class set contains each class only once. For example, detector labels` Crack, Crack, Live_Knot` and Gemini labels` Crack, Live_Knot` produce the same set. Repeated boxes for one class do not create a disagreement.


The final` parsed_result` keeps Gemini’s response when the selected route is a recognized Gemini route, the detector data and response values are valid, and neither the model nor the parser reports an error. All other cases receive a fallback: an empty` visible_classes` list,` assessment="unclear"` , the reason` Invalid or unavailable response` , and` parser_error=true` . This includes the initial human-review route.


Here,` parser_error` acts as a combined status flag for all these fallback conditions. The fallback prevents an unavailable or invalid automated result from being returned as` no_visible_defect` .


A valid Gemini response that says` unclear` or disagrees with the detector is retained and flagged for review. The review decision and the assessment therefore serve different purposes. Likewise,` needs_review=false` means these checks did not flag the case; the detector and Gemini may still agree that a visible defect is present.


The block returns the inspection ID, routing reason, selected model, parsed result, review flag, and review reason. It also returns the detected classes and confidence scores as JSON strings, the final assessment, and the` collect` flag used by the collection path in Step 9.


Use the following code in the` inspection_decision` Custom Python block:


Python


```text
def   run  (self, route, bundle, predictions, inspection_id, invalid, critical):
import   json
import   math
import   numpy   as   np


allowed   =   {
"Crack"  ,   "Marrow"  ,   "Resin"  ,   "Dead_Knot"  ,
"Knot_with_Crack"  ,   "Quartzity"  ,   "Live_Knot"  ,   "Knot_Missing"  ,
}
route   =   route   if   isinstance  (route,   str  )   else   ""
known_route   =   route   in   {  "flash_lite"  ,   "flash"  ,   "pro"  ,   "human"  }


# Do not read predictions that the routing block has already rejected.
names   =   []
score_list   =   []
prediction_error   =   bool  (invalid)


if   not   prediction_error:
try  :
names   =   list  (predictions.data.get(  "class_name"  , []))
scores   =   predictions.confidence
score_list   =   [  float  (x)   for   x   in   scores]   if   scores   is   not   None   else   []
count   =   len  (predictions)


if   len  (names)   !=   count   or   len  (score_list)   !=   count:
raise   ValueError  (  "Missing class names or confidence scores"  )
if   any  (  not   isinstance  (x,   str  )   or   x   not   in   allowed   for   x   in   names):
raise   ValueError  (  "Unsupported detector class"  )
if   any  (  not   math.isfinite(x)   or   not   0   <=   x   <=   1   for   x   in   score_list):
raise   ValueError  (  "Invalid detector confidence"  )
except   Exception  :
prediction_error   =   True
names   =   []
score_list   =   []


# Read the selected branch's response and error flags.
b   =   bundle   if   isinstance  (bundle,   dict  )   else   {}
model   =   str  (b.get(  "model"  )   or   "none"  )
raw   =   b.get(  "visible_classes"  )
assessment   =   b.get(  "assessment"  )
reason   =   b.get(  "reason"  )
failed   =   bool  (b.get(  "parser_error"  ,   True  )   or   b.get(  "model_error"  ,   True  ))


valid   =   (
isinstance  (raw,   list  )
and   all  (  isinstance  (x,   str  )   and   x   in   allowed   for   x   in   raw)
and   isinstance  (assessment,   str  )
and   assessment   in   (  "visible_defect"  ,   "no_visible_defect"  ,   "unclear"  )
and   isinstance  (reason,   str  )
and   bool  (reason.strip())
)
if   valid   and   assessment   !=   "unclear"  :
if   (assessment   ==   "visible_defect"  )   !=   (  len  (raw)   >   0  ):
valid   =   False


# Describe the route chosen by select_route.
if   route   ==   "human"  :
route_reason   =   "Invalid prediction data, unexpected class, or no matching rule"
elif   route   ==   "pro"  :
route_reason   =   (
"Critical class present"
if   critical   else   "Detection confidence below 0.60"
)
elif   route   ==   "flash"  :
route_reason   =   "Detection confidence below 0.90"
elif   route   ==   "flash_lite"  :
if   prediction_error:
route_reason   =   "Flash-Lite selected, but detector predictions are invalid"
else  :
route_reason   =   (
"No detections; full-image verification required"
if   not   names   else   "All detector confidences at least 0.90"
)
else  :
route_reason   =   "Unexpected route"


# Request review for invalid routes, predictions, or model responses.
problems   =   []
if   not   known_route:
problems.append(  "Unexpected route"  )
if   prediction_error:
problems.append(  "Invalid or unreadable detector predictions"  )


if   route   ==   "human"  :
if   not   problems:
problems.append(route_reason)
elif   not   problems:
if   failed   or   not   valid:
problems.append(
"Gemini or JSON parsing failure, or invalid required response values"
)
else  :
if   assessment   ==   "unclear"  :
problems.append(  "Gemini assessment unclear: "   +   reason.strip())
if   set  (raw)   !=   set  (names):
problems.append(  "Gemini classes disagree with detector classes"  )


# Keep the response only when the automated result is usable.
usable   =   (
valid
and   not   failed
and   not   prediction_error
and   known_route
and   route   !=   "human"
)
clean   =   {
"visible_classes"  : raw   if   usable   else   [],
"assessment"  : assessment   if   usable   else   "unclear"  ,
"reason"  : reason   if   usable   else   "Invalid or unavailable response"  ,
"parser_error"  :   bool  (
failed   or   not   valid   or   prediction_error
or   not   known_route   or   route   ==   "human"
),
}
needs_review   =   bool  (problems)


# Each remaining Flash-Lite case has a 5% chance of collection.
collect   =   (
route   in   (  "pro"  ,   "human"  )
or   needs_review
or   (route   ==   "flash_lite"   and   np.random.random()   <   0.05  )
)


return   {
"inspection_id"  :   str  (inspection_id),
"routing_reason"  : route_reason,
"selected_model"  : model,
"parsed_result"  : clean,
"needs_review"  : needs_review,
"review_reason"  :   "; "  .join(problems),
"collect"  :   bool  (collect),
"detected_classes"  : json.dumps(names),
"detected_confidences"  : json.dumps(score_list),
"assessment"  : clean[  "assessment"  ],
}
```


**Figure 4. Response validation and class-set comparison determine whether human review is required.**


### Step 8: Create the annotated image and inspection outputs


Add` bounding_box_visualization` using the original image and` wood_detector.predictions` . Connect its image output to` label_visualization` , use the same predictions, and select` Class and Confidence` for the label text.


Then add a Text Display block named` route_banner` . Use the labeled image as its input and show the selected route, Gemini model, and review flag across the top of the image. Use this template for the banner:


```text
ROUTE: {{ $parameters.route }} | {{ $parameters.model }} | REVIEW: {{ $parameters.review }}
```


Map the banner parameters as follows:


- ` route` →` $steps.select_route.output`
- ` model` →` $steps.inspection_decision.selected_model`
- ` review` →` $steps.inspection_decision.needs_review`


The annotated image retains the original detector boxes, class names, and per-box confidence scores. The banner makes the route and review decision visible alongside those detections. Expose the following Workflow outputs:


Output What it contains


` inspection_id` The ID supplied by the calling application.


` predictions` Original detector predictions.


` output_image` Annotated image with the route banner.


` selected_route` The route chosen for the image.


` routing_reason` Why the route was selected, or a problem identified with that route.


` selected_gemini_model` Model identifier from the selected branch, or` none` for the human branch or an unavailable model identifier.


` parsed_gemini_result` Validated Gemini response, or an` unclear` fallback when no usable automated response is available.


` needs_review` Whether the case needs human review.


` review_reason` Why human review was requested.


` collection_requested` Whether the enabled collection gate selected the image.


` collection_status` Message from the upload block when it runs.


` collection_error` Upload error status when the block runs.


The calling application can use` inspection_id` to link these outputs to the original inspection. Read` parsed_gemini_result` together with` needs_review` and` review_reason` to understand both the assessment and whether a person needs to check it. The next step configures the collection outputs.


### Step 9: Collect useful images for retraining


The` Inspection_Decision` block also decides whether an image is useful for collection. It selects Pro referrals, initial human cases, and any case flagged for review, including class disagreements. Each remaining Flash-Lite case has a 5% chance of being selected for collection.


This sampling happens in the custom block. The upload block is not configured to sample 5% of all incoming images.


Add an Expression block named` collection_switch` that returns` true` only when both` inspection_decision.collect` and` enable_collection` are` true` . Connect it to` gate_collection` , a Continue If block whose next step is` collect_for_review` .


Use a[Roboflow Dataset Upload block (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/data-storage/roboflow-dataset-upload?ref=blog.roboflow.com) for` collect_for_review` and configure these settings:


Setting Value


Image` $inputs.image`


Target project` wood-surface-defect-detection`


Labeling batch prefix` wood_router_review`


Usage quota name` wood_defect_router_review_upload`


Persist predictions` false`


Fire and forget` false`


With` persist_predictions=false` , uploaded images do not carry detector predictions as annotations. With` fire_and_forget=false` , the upload is synchronous: the Workflow waits for it to finish so the upload message and error status can be checked.


Add` inspection_id` and` detector_model` to the upload metadata so each collected image can be linked to its inspection and detector. To keep a fuller record for retraining analysis, have the calling application save the routing and review outputs alongside the inspection ID.


Map` collection_requested` to` collection_switch.output` ,` collection_status` to` collect_for_review.message` , and` collection_error` to` collect_for_review.error_status` . A request to collect an image does not prove that it was uploaded; check the status and error outputs when the upload block runs.


Collection stays off while` enable_collection=false` . When enabled, the single gated upload path prevents multiple collection paths within one execution, even if a Pro referral also has a class disagreement. It does not remove duplicates across repeated inspections or neighboring video frames.


### Step 10: Prepare the optional human-review handoff


Add a Continue If block named` gate_webhook` that checks` inspection_decision.needs_review` . Connect it to a[Webhook Sink (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/data-storage/webhook-sink?ref=blog.roboflow.com) named` review_webhook` . Configure the sink to send a POST request containing the inspection ID, route, selected model, parsed result, review flag, and review reason.

The calling application must also handle detector or Gemini request failures and unhandled exceptions. These can stop execution before a review result is returned and must be treated as failed inspections requiring attention, never as clean panels.

## Measure the Results and Improve the Detector


Compare the router with a baseline that sends every image to one selected Gemini model. Record how often each route runs, how many cases need human review, missed defects, false alarms, and total processing time.


Include the detector, the model calls actually made, and external review work when calculating costs. The outputs we defined track inspection decisions and collection status. Record processing time and billing details separately in the calling application or its monitoring system. Fewer Pro calls alone do not establish a lower total cost.


Use the collected images to identify recurring problems, such as uncertain cracks, disagreements about knots, or wood appearances that the detector has not learned well. Annotate and review suitable images, then[generate a new dataset version (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/versions/dataset-versions/create-a-dataset-version?ref=blog.roboflow.com) and train an updated model. A dataset version is a fixed snapshot; adding collected images does not automatically update an existing training version.


Finally,[evaluate the updated detector (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/models/evaluate/evaluate-trained-models?ref=blog.roboflow.com) and test the routing policy again. Retraining can change the predictions and the distribution of confidence scores, which can change how often each branch is selected.


## Conclusion


Model routing uses the detector's results to choose the next step for each wood inspection. Routine images can receive a lightweight check, selected conditions can receive more detailed analysis, and uncertain results can be flagged for a person.


Build and test the policy in[Roboflow Workflows (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows?ref=blog.roboflow.com) , choose thresholds using reviewed inspection results, and use collected cases to improve the detector over time.


You might also be interested in reading about[model cascades](https://roboflow.com/blog/model-cascades-for-computer-vision?ref=blog.roboflow.com) and[model evaluation](https://roboflow.com/blog/compare-trained-models?ref=blog.roboflow.com) .
